chapters.title: Chapter 4: From Raw Data to Usable Signal

lessons.title: Feature Engineering for Alternative Data Signals

body.text: A clean number is not a feature. A feature is a clean number that has been made comparable across time and across companies, which is a completely different and much harder job.

children.text: Cleaning, covered in Lesson 1, and point-in-time discipline, covered in Lesson 2, get you to a trustworthy raw number. This lesson turns that number into something a model can actually use: normalized so it is comparable, deseasonalized so calendar effects don't masquerade as signal, smoothed so noise doesn't dominate, and standardized so it means the same thing across every company in your universe.
From Raw Metric to Feature: The Normalization Step

A raw count almost never means what it looks like it means until you know what it should be divided by. A larger company generates more web traffic, more e-way bills, and more job postings simply because it is larger, not because anything interesting is happening. The fix is always the same shape: pick a sensible denominator before comparing anything.

body.caption: The raw number is rarely the feature, what you divide it by usually is

cells: Comparing absolute registration counts across two auto makers of very different sizes
Registrations as a percentage change versus the same calendar period a year earlier, for the same company
Treating a rising traffic count as growing demand without checking the baseline
Traffic indexed to a fixed base period, so you are tracking relative change, not an absolute estimate you already know is noisy
E-way bill volume for a company's sector
Comparing a large-cap manufacturer's e-way bill count directly against a small-cap peer's
E-way bill volume normalized per unit of the company's last reported revenue base

children.text: Removing the Calendar: Deseasonalizing and Year-on-Year Comparisons

Chapter 2 showed you gold search interest spiking around Dhanteras and e-way bill volume spiking around Diwali. Those are genuine, recurring calendar effects, not noise, but comparing this week's raw level to last week's raw level will misread every one of them as a trend when it is really the calendar repeating itself. The standard fix is a year-on-year comparison against the same calendar period, which cancels out the recurring seasonal pattern and isolates the part of the change that is actually new information.

body.caption: Comparing against the same period one year earlier cancels out recurring seasonal and calendar effects that a simple week-over-week or month-over-month comparison would misread as a trend.

body.title: Calculate the Year-on-Year Feature
body.prompt: An auto ancillary company's e-way bill volume index this March is 118. The same index for the same company last March was 100. What is the year-on-year growth, as a percentage?
body.explanation: YoY Growth = (118 - 100) / 100 = 0.18, or 18%. Because both values are measured for the same calendar month a year apart, this comparison already cancels out any recurring seasonal pattern specific to March, isolating the genuinely new 18% of growth.

children.text: Smoothing Noise: Rolling Windows and Point-in-Time Lags

Chapter 1's VAHAN case study flagged that daily registration counts are noisy: batch registration by dealers and inconsistent RTO data entry mean a single day's number is not fully trustworthy on its own. A rolling average, seven or thirty days depending on how quickly you need to react, smooths that noise into something more stable. The one discipline you cannot skip is respecting the knowledge date from the previous lesson: a rolling window computed as of a historical decision date must only include observations whose knowledge date had already passed by that point, or you have quietly reintroduced look-ahead bias through the back door of a moving average.
Level vs Rate of Change: Which One Is the Actual Signal?

The level of a metric and its rate of change carry different information, and which one matters depends on where the company sits in its life cycle. For a large, mature company, the absolute level of web traffic is high and structurally stable, so a small percentage change is often the meaningful event. For a newer, fast-growing company, the trajectory of growth itself is the story, and the current level tells you comparatively little on its own.

body.title: Level or Rate of Change?
body.question: You are building a feature to track a five-year-old, fast-scaling e-commerce company that is still roughly doubling its user base annually, using web and app traffic data. Should your feature emphasize the absolute traffic level or the rate of change in traffic?
options: The absolute level, since bigger is always better regardless of company stage
The rate of change, since the company's story is fundamentally about the trajectory of growth, not a stable baseline level
Neither matters, only fundamental data should be used for a young company
Always use the level for every company, regardless of stage, for consistency
body.explanation: A company that is still roughly doubling annually is defined by its growth trajectory, not a settled baseline level. The rate of change captures whether that trajectory is accelerating, holding steady, or decelerating, which is exactly the kind of information that would move a valuation built on continued fast growth. For a large, mature company with a stable base, the level itself would carry more relative weight.

children.text: Cross-Sectional Standardization: Z-Scores and Percentile Ranks

markDefs.definition: A way of expressing a company's feature value relative to its peer group at the same point in time, measured in standard deviations from the peer group's mean. A z-score of 2 means the value is two standard deviations above the average of the comparison group.

children.text: An 18% year-on-year growth number means very little on its own, it needs context from peers measured the same way, at the same time. Converting a raw feature into a

against the cross-section of comparable companies, or equivalently a percentile rank, makes the feature comparable across your universe and stable even if the raw metric's typical scale shifts over time.

body.caption: x is the company's feature value, mu is the cross-sectional mean across the comparison group at the same point in time, sigma is the cross-sectional standard deviation.

body.title: Calculate the Cross-Sectional Z-Score
body.prompt: Across a peer group of auto ancillary companies, the average year-on-year e-way bill growth is 8%, with a standard deviation of 5 percentage points. The company from the earlier exercise posted 18% year-on-year growth. What is its z-score, to one decimal place?
body.explanation: z = (18 - 8) / 5 = 10 / 5 = 2.0. This company's e-way bill growth sits two standard deviations above its peer group's average, which is a genuinely notable reading rather than an ordinary one, and it is this standardized score, not the raw 18%, that should feed into a cross-sectional ranking or a composite signal alongside other features.

body.text: A single well-built feature, normalized, deseasonalized, and cross-sectionally standardized, is worth more than five raw metrics thrown into a model unprocessed. Chapter 5 picks up from here and shows how to combine several such features into an actual research signal.
The company and peer group figures in this lesson are illustrative teaching examples, not reported data for any real company. Nothing here is a recommendation to trade any security.

points: A raw alternative data metric is rarely a usable feature on its own, it needs a sensible denominator so it is comparable across companies of different sizes
Year-on-year comparisons against the same calendar period cancel out recurring seasonal effects, such as festival-linked spikes, that a simple period-over-period comparison would misread as a trend
Rolling windows smooth genuinely noisy alternative data, but every rolling calculation used in a backtest must still respect the knowledge date discipline from the previous lesson

Whether the level or the rate of change of a metric matters most depends on the company's stage, mature companies are often better read through small percentage changes, fast-growing companies through their growth trajectory
Cross-sectional z-scores or percentile ranks make a feature comparable across your universe and stable over time, converting a raw percentage into a standardized, genuinely informative reading
This lesson turns a clean, point-in-time-correct number into a real feature, Chapter 5 covers how to combine several such features into a tested, tradable signal
